prop: Each typed leg ships with the presentation it was measured with, including its splitter, because the numbers belong to the presentation and not to the model. The `fact` gate (`pick_cls`) splits into sentences, asks one `choice` over them plus NONE and one CURRENT/PROPOSED/ARGUMENT `choice` per sentence, and scores the sum of each sentence's pick probability times its P(CURRENT). The `claim` gate (`pick_clause`) cuts every sentence at every `,` `;` `:` or dash, with no bracket awareness, asks one `choice` over the clauses plus NONE, and scores 1 - P(NONE). Jev classify on `claim` cuts clauses only outside brackets and code spans. Both gates put the subject's text before its evidence; both carry NOT_A_DISAGREEMENT, ported from CHECK_SYSTEM, in NONE's criterion. A port that "improves" any of these — one splitter for both, a shared score — is an unmeasured configuration.

Decision — routing and credential. A model value whose vendor half is exactly `typesafe` is sent to TypeSafe's endpoint (a second constant beside `ENDPOINT`, https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone) with a credential read only from the environment variable TYPESAFE_API_KEY, on the same terms `KEY_VARS` states for OpenRouter's: never a config key, never written. Every other value keeps going to OpenRouter unchanged. `is_model_name` already accepts `typesafe/jev-1.13.0`, so the routing needs no new value syntax. `verify.model` refuses a `typesafe/` value at `config set`, through a new `Accepts` variant, because the check leg must be an LLM and a refusal at `config set` can never suppress a mint, where a refusal at mint time would.

When code proposes the literal candidates and the shipped filters run unchanged, Jev judging them matches the LLM literal leg on the same 88 claims at a sixth of the cost: 82% precision and 18% recall (9 of 11 flagged claims later needed work) against the LLM's 80% and 16% (8 of 10), at $0.00023 a draw against $0.00132, with 17 of 21 literals raised in every draw against 6 of 29. Added to the check leg alone, either literal leg raises the supports-only claims flagged from 4 of 38 to 5 or 6, over the 11.3% steering-hazard line; behind the Jev claim gate, check plus Jev literals flags 4 of 38 and 20 of 50 claims that needed work, against 18 for the check alone. That joint figure is computed against the August check-leg flags, not a joint run.

Decision — one new key, `verify.typed_model`, not a `verify.provider` and not one key per leg. A provider key would describe a switch that cannot exist: whatever it is set to, the check leg stays on OpenRouter. One key per leg would each have to be printed in every response and each have to earn its place, for legs that never run apart from a per-verb table. Unset, the verifier is byte-identical to today. Set to a `typesafe/` value, it enables the typed legs that a per-verb table in source names for each verb — the same status `classify_system_for` already gives the classify prompt — and every response prints it as `typed_model`, beside the version the endpoint resolved it to.

Decision — credential and budget. With a `typesafe/` value set and TYPESAFE_API_KEY absent, the verification reports `unauthorized` and the `missing` diagnostic gains an arm naming TYPESAFE_API_KEY; it never falls back to running the LLM legs while printing a typed model it did not use. Typed legs get their own per-leg budget constant instead of `DEFAULT_MS_PER_LEG`'s 60 seconds, which `expected_calls` multiplies into the default timeout: one Jev draw over 16 findings had a median latency of 0.69 seconds and a maximum of 1.01, so three typed legs at 60 seconds each would quadruple a budget for calls that take about a second.

prop: `scope.rs` states its own residual gap in terms that name the semantic verifier's job: of the two overreaching facts that motivated it, it catches one, and the one it misses (F7, "mirrors the server's" over an extent covering only the client) is missed because the overreach names no location at all — "invisible to any check of this shape". Its rejected refinement is recorded with the same reason: naming a symbol the read code calls is normal while concluding about what that symbol does is the failure, and "those two are not distinguishable by string matching." A check that compares meaning rather than location is therefore aimed at a gap the existing check documents rather than at a new speculation.

The supports-only claims flagged do not separate the two classifiers by more than the check leg's own drift between runs. The steering-hazard line is defined over claims — 7 of 62 — and counted that way Jev's arm flags 8 and the LLM's 6, on either side of it. Counted per draw, the two differ by two draws: 24 of 185 (13.0%) with Jev's labels against 22 of 185 (11.9%) with the LLM's; while the same LLM classify-and-check configuration moved from 18 of 183 (9.8%) in August to 22 of 185 today. The line's verdict on Jev classify therefore rests on a difference smaller than the variation of the configuration it is compared against, and is not settled by these runs.

The eval settles which approach to build and settles nothing about whether to build it. It settles the approach: on 15 cases run 3 times, the one-call direct comparison caught 32/33 planted defects and left 12/12 sound claims alone at $0.0060, against 28/32 and 7/12 at $0.0532 for the three-call extract-then-judge pipeline — better on both axes at a ninth of the cost, so the pipeline hypothesis did not survive measurement. It settles nothing about value, by its own statement: the case set is small, self-authored and synthetic with no case taken from a real memo, one case was found mislabeled by the model disagreeing with it, and "Nothing here measures whether warning an author earlier removes a grounding round, which is the actual cost argument."

As the refuter on `fact`, Jev performs within the range of the two LLM refuters measured on the same 16 adjudicated `contradicts` findings, at under a hundredth of their cost: Jev (3-draw majority) keeps 8 of 10 true catches at 80% precision, against Sonnet's 8 of 10 at 89% and Gemini's 10 of 10 at 77%; one Jev draw cost $0.0018 for all 16 findings (README: $0.00011 a finding, against $0.0228 and $0.0184), with a median latency of 0.69 seconds.

The extract-then-compare pipeline should remain selectable despite losing the measurement, because it holds one property the winner cannot have and that property is about auditability rather than accuracy: its findings are re-derivable by anyone holding the two extracted records, with no model in the loop, whereas the direct comparison's findings are not re-derivable without a model. Its accuracy numbers (17/30 caught, 11/12 left alone) were taken on the earlier 14-case set and so are not comparable with the 15-case columns, which means the case for keeping it must rest on that property and not on its score.

Decision — what the gate does to a verification. The gate asks its question first, of the subject's text and evidence alone, before any classify call, which is how it was measured. Below the verb's threshold, no classify and no check call is made and the verification reports a new status, `gated`, never `ok` with an empty findings list: `Status` exists so that nothing empty passes for a clean result. The literal leg, when on, still runs on a gated subject, since it answers a different question and the measured join shows literals-always-run at 20 of 50 needed-work claims flagged against 19 with literals gated, both at 4 of 38 sound. A gate that fails — transport, timeout, an unreadable reply — never skips: the check runs, and the response carries `gate_incomplete` the way it carries `literals_incomplete` today. The gate's probability is never shown to the author; `Finding` carries no confidence score by design, and a verification should not either.

prop: Rejected, each on its own measurement: a gate asked of the whole note (`whole`: -1% net on `fact`, 8% on `claim`); gate criteria rewritten for recall, dropping CHECK_SYSTEM's exclusions (`pick_recall`: 44% net on `fact` against `pick`'s 52%, and AUC 0.59 on `prose` against 0.65); the capture placed before the author's text (`pick_evfirst`: 20% net on `fact`); and a gate on `prose`, where no variant exceeds AUC 0.69. A Jev gate in front of the check leg is worth having on `fact` and `claim` but not on `prose`, and what makes it worth having is asking which unit disagrees rather than whether anything does. prop: The warning should be carried as a top-level `verify` OBJECT in the mint result, not a fourth array beside `attention` and `overlap`. `mcp.rs` establishes the array form for a reason that holds here — "the caller is a program, and a field it can branch on beats a string it has to notice" — but `attention` and `overlap` are derived per call from workspace state already on disk, so empty and absent mean the same thing for them. A verifier can fail to run, and "found nothing" must be distinguishable from "did not look". An object with a mandatory `status` field carrying exactly one of `ok`, `off`, `unavailable`, `timeout`, `unauthorized`, and a `findings` array that is meaningful only when `status` is `ok`, makes that distinction branchable; a bare array cannot express it.

Decision — the refuter. `verify.refuter_model` accepts a `typesafe/` value, answered as one `choice` over CORRECT, WRONG and UNCLEAR with REFUTE_SYSTEM's own criteria, the measured port; only WRONG drops, unchanged. The default refuter stays the LLM it is: Jev's refuter numbers cover `fact`'s `contradicts` findings only. The self-refutation guard in `refute_findings`, which today compares the refuter only against `verify.model`, extends to `verify.typed_model`: when both name the same model, the refuter is not run over `unevidenced` findings that model judged, and `tel.detail` says so as the existing branch does. A refuter call that fails keeps its finding, as today, and the response names the failure as `refuter_incomplete`, so that unrefuted findings do not reach an author under a printed `refuter_model`.

prop: The independence argument that rescued `Domain ⊆ Extent` transfers to a semantic mint-time verifier. `scope.rs` records that the comparison was abandoned as vacuous because one author supplying both sides produced byte-identical results about 80% of the time — "Independence, not capture, was what moved that number" — and that what fixed it was making one side captured by the tool (extent, with deliberately no flag to type one in) and the other authored (the note). A claim's proposition is authored by the same hand; its cited facts' captured output was recorded by `look`/`run` under the same no-typed-input rule. So the two sides of a proposition-versus-captured-output comparison are independent by the same construction, not by the author's diligence.

The implementation surface is src/verify.rs and src/config.rs, plus docs/verify.md. The declared `Status` is the verifier's enum at src/verify.rs:120 — a different `pub enum Status`, a ledger row's, sits at src/model.rs:46 and is not touched. `run()` in src/verify.rs is modified too, to place the gate before classify and route classify by verb; it is not declared as a target, because a whole-worktree census of the symbol `run` would match nearly every file. prop: Shipping this falsifies one of `lib.rs`'s two pinned whole-crate properties, and the correct replacement is a per-command row rather than a weakened sentence — which is what the module's own preamble already prescribes, having recorded that "a single sentence about the whole crate was wrong for months" and having restated the write list per command for exactly that reason. The property that breaks is "there are no network calls anywhere, which the dependency set enforces rather than the prose": once an HTTP client is linked, the dependency set no longer enforces anything and the sentence would be prose pretending to be an invariant. The replacement row names the reaching commands — `fact`, `claim` and `prose` may make one outbound call to the configured provider, and only when enabled with a key in the environment — and states that `check`, `brief`, `query`, `review`, `workspaces`, `render`, `record` and `config` make none. The crate's other pinned property, that nothing here ever executes a command named by a document, is untouched and is the reason `check` must not be a reaching command.

Two results kill the feature, and both must be declared before the test is run. First, low recall against the verdicts that cost a round: if the verifier surfaces fewer than a quarter of the 23 refutes on their first-render wording, it does not catch the findings that force a revision round, and the whole cost argument — that warning earlier removes a grounding round — fails on the only corpus that could show it. Second, false-positive load: if the verifier flags more than one in ten of the 578 supporting claims at their first-render wording, it is a steering hazard, since the recipient is usually an agent that will act on a warning and each such flag is an invitation to damage a claim that was already sound. Either result kills it regardless of how the other lands, and a run that is merely disappointing on `qualifies` — the largest bucket at 185 — is not a kill, because a qualification is often a legitimate scope narrowing rather than a defect.

Decision — the per-verb table carries only what was measured on that verb. `fact`: a gate asked as a `choice` over sentences with per-sentence classification (`pick_cls`), skipping below 0.45; classify stays on the LLM, because the Jev port of the classify prompt `fact` shares with `claim` was never run on `fact`; the literal leg's judgement stays on the LLM, because `literal_findings` takes no verb and Jev's literal judgement was measured on claims only. `claim`: a gate asked as a `choice` over clauses (`pick_clause`), skipping below 0.53; classify by Jev, over clauses cut outside brackets and code spans, a clause counting as current at P(current) >= 0.4; the literal leg judged by Jev when `verify.literals` is on. `prose`: no typed leg, since no gate presentation separated and prose is off by default. The two gates are different presentations, not one gate with two thresholds: `pick_cls` saves 7% on `claim` against `pick_clause`'s 21%.
This design was built against the tetel repository at commit 57bd0e29a6c8bd3861f3982bebe3486f80e0453d with a clean working tree; every code citation below refers to that state.

TET-28's "workspace-rooted" requirement is NOT decidable from today's capture in the case that matters most. When look_grep finds matches, it records one extent entry per matched file, keyed on that file's resolved path, with label "<file> (grep: <pattern>)" — and the search root appears nowhere in what is captured; the code's own comment says the entries are keyed "not by the search root or the grep command line". A repo-wide grep and a single-file grep that matched the same file therefore capture byte-identical extents. Every genuine census of a symbol an implementer is told to modify falls in this positive-match case, because the symbol's definition site matches.

Only `claim` should be checked by default, with `fact` and `prose` available through `verify.verbs` but off. `claim` is the verb the eval actually measured — its cases imitate "the shape of a tetel claim and its captured evidence" — so it is the only one of the three whose accuracy numbers mean anything. `fact` is partly covered already, deterministically and for free, by the `scope` check, and the semantic residue it would add is real but is the smaller of the two halves `scope.rs` describes. `prose` is the highest-volume verb of the three in the largest memo measured (130 log lines against 114 for claims and 33 for facts), and comparing prose against claim propositions is a different comparison from the one measured, with no numbers behind it at all. Defaulting it on would spend the largest share of the latency budget on the least-evidenced comparison.

The zero-match case IS decidable today, and it shows the shape the fix should take: a no-match grep records one entry whose key is the resolved search root and whose Marker { root, state } is resolved from that same root, so "was this bounded negative repo-wide" reduces to comparing two tool-captured strings on one entry — key versus world_root. TET-5's per-observation markers and the unconditional -H made this comparison meaningful; they did not extend it to the positive-match case.

The census therefore needs a small capture extension before any refusal can exist: look_grep should record, for every search, one root-level search entry — key = the resolved search root, a label carrying the pattern and the match-file count, marker resolved from the search root — alongside the existing per-file match entries, making the match and no-match cases uniform. "Workspace-rooted" then has one decidable definition covering both cases: the search entry's key equals its own world_root, a byte comparison of two strings the same look_grep call captured from the same canonicalized directory. No author-typed input participates on either side.

A census check cannot be built on labels, and the record model already shows the right way to extend the schema. At mint time only key, label, world_root and world_state survive into an ExtentEntry — the observation's kind is dropped, and the grep pattern exists only inside a display label, where an author-chosen pattern containing " in " or "(grep: " would make parsing ambiguous. The census therefore needs the new root-level search entry to carry two structured fields into ExtentEntry — the observation kind and the search pattern — following the exact precedent world_root set: #[serde(default)], with the empty value read as "predates the field, not eligible" rather than guessed about. Legacy facts can then never satisfy a census requirement, whose remedy is precisely to re-run the grep under the new capture. The snapshot already ships facts.jsonl with full extent entries, so check reads these fields from files every snapshot already contains; and because no surface lets an author supply an extent by hand, both sides of the rooting comparison and the pattern are tool-captured by construction.

A mention-triggered refusal (candidate 2) is off-charter and already measured dead in this repository. The charter forbids heuristic refusals outright, and scope.rs records the measurement: string-matching symbol references was tried for the note-outside-extent check and rejected because it "would have flagged a legitimate quotation ... while missing both real overreaches" — naming a symbol is normal, concluding about it is the failure, "and those two are not distinguishable by string matching". A refusal wired to that detector would refuse honest memos, which is precisely what scope.rs's "refusing would make the honest case unwritable" disposition exists to prevent. This also means the README Direction entry for this feature — "requiring a workspace-rooted search behind a claim that names a symbol" — is phrased as the mention-triggered shape and should be corrected to the declared-target shape when this ships.

The decidable trigger is declaration (candidate 1): a modification target is a structured record the author creates — a symbol string plus a fact citation — and the refusal fires only on a declared target whose cited fact carries no qualifying census entry. This sits inside the machine partition's own stated principle, that machine failures are "objective contradictions between a document and the record it claims to rest on, decidable without a human": a target row is exactly a pointer at evidence, and "you did not point at your evidence" is the README's own example of a decidable question. The refusal's remedy is singular — run the workspace-rooted grep for that symbol, mint the fact, cite it (or withdraw the target) — so refusal rather than report is the right disposition for the declared-but-uncensused case, by the same discriminator under which scope.rs chose report: there, only a person can tell context from conclusion; here, nothing is left to tell.

Under-declaration — the memo recommends modifying a symbol it never declared — cannot be a refusal and must not be silently absorbed either. Deciding from prose that a sentence "tells an implementer to modify X" is a heuristic read of English, exactly the class the charter routes to the human-owed partition or nowhere; scope.rs's measured precedent shows the symbol-detector that trigger would need flags quotation and misses conclusion. The design therefore makes the omission visible instead of detected: (a) once a workspace declares any target, render emits a Modification targets section, and once any claim exists it emits the section even when empty — "Modification targets: none declared" — so a memo that recommends changes while declaring nothing shows a hole where the census should be, in front of every reader; and (b) check's standing non-coverage list, whose first entry is already "dependents that never declared themselves", gains a census-specific line ("a recommendation whose target was never declared") so the blind spot is printed rather than implicit.

Invariants, each paired with the revert that must turn its test red; demonstration is owed when the code exists. (1) With `verify.typed_model` unset, a verification makes the same calls in the same order and prints the same fields as today — revert: default `typed_model` to a typesafe value. (2) A subject scored below its verb's gate threshold reports status `gated`, and no classify or check call is made — revert: return `ok` with empty findings. (3) A gate call that fails runs the check, and the response carries `gate_incomplete` — revert: treat a failed gate as a skip. (4) `config set verify.model typesafe/jev-1.13.0` is refused — revert: accept any model name for `verify.model`. (5) With `typed_model` and `refuter_model` naming the same model, the refuter is not run over `unevidenced` findings that model judged, and `tel.detail` says so — revert: compare the refuter against `verify.model` only. (6) With a `typesafe/` value set and TYPESAFE_API_KEY absent, the status is `unauthorized` and the message names TYPESAFE_API_KEY — revert: fall back to the LLM legs. (7) A reply whose resolved `model` differs from the measured constant adds `typed_model_unmeasured` — revert: compare against the configured alias. (8) `fact` never runs Jev classify or Jev literal judgement, and `prose` runs no typed leg — revert: one table row for every verb.

prop: A finding must name the failing clause and quote the captured evidence rather than assert a verdict, and the eval supplies the reason as a measured case rather than a worry. The three-call pipeline's false positives were all one failure mode — the extractor drops a binding and the judge cannot tell a dropped binding from an absent one — and the recorded instance is a finding that reported "the evidence contains no `pin` name or binding" against evidence whose lines 425-436 are the pin computation. That finding is a verdict: a recipient can only accept or ignore it. Had it named the clause it was judging and quoted the evidence lines it judged against, its wrongness would have been visible in one step to a reader with the memo in front of them. So each entry carries the quoted clause, the fact id and the quoted span it was compared against, and no confidence score — the recipient is usually an agent that will act on a warning, and a verdict invites compliance where a quotation invites checking.

Where the refusal lives: at declaration, then re-verified at check. The `target` verb refuses to create a target whose cited fact carries no qualifying census entry — the same authoring-time shape as fact refusing on an empty pending buffer ("a fact needs a preceding look/run"; a target needs a preceding rooted census). Because a fact's extent is immutable once minted and a target is immutable once declared, this makes "every declared target is censused" a workspace invariant, and no render-path refusal is needed for workspace-authored documents; render's job is only to emit the targets section. check independently re-verifies the rendered document against its snapshot and reports [uncensused-target] as a machine failure in the partition's scope line, which is what catches a hand-authored or tampered document that never passed through the refusing verb. Like notes_outside_extent and mint_windows, that check runs only when a snapshot ships; without one, target rows are reported human-owed as unverifiable, consistent with the standing choice that a missing snapshot is human-owed rather than a machine failure. The verb must be one dispatch shared by CLI and MCP, the pattern look and fact already use, because this codebase has recorded a CLI/MCP drift on exactly such a duplicated act.

The rooting predicate — census entry's key byte-equals its own world_root — is satisfiable and fails closed. On this machine and repo the two spellings (fs-canonicalized search root; git rev-parse --show-toplevel) agree byte-for-byte, so an honestly rooted grep satisfies the predicate; and if the two tools ever disagree on spelling, the mismatch refuses an honest census loudly rather than accepting an unrooted one silently, because inequality can only ever deny rooting, never grant it. Two hardenings belong in the implementation: look_grep should itself compare the canonicalized search root against the marker's root at capture time and store the search entry's key in the marker's spelling when they name the same directory, so check stays a pure byte comparison; and the agreement should be pinned by a test, since one probe on one machine shows the common case, not an invariant.

The qualifying-census predicate, fully: a declared target (symbol S, citing fact F) is censused iff F's captured extent contains a search entry whose kind field says it is a whole-search record, whose pattern field byte-equals S, whose key byte-equals its own world_root, and whose world_root is git-backed (neither the no-git sentinel nor the empty predates-the-field value). Byte-equality of pattern to symbol is the only sound decidable comparison available: grep is invoked with the pattern verbatim (-e <pattern>), so a looser rule like "pattern contains the symbol" would accept a grep whose pattern merely embeds S in a longer string and therefore matches a strict subset of S's textual occurrences, while anything semantically wider would require deciding containment between regular expressions. Symbols that are not literal strings in the system grep's dialect are a stated limit of the census, not a case the check adjudicates.

The census's blind spots are boundable from what the capture actually does, and belong in check's printed non-coverage: (a) a textual grep cannot see dynamic dispatch, re-exports and aliased imports, or macro-generated and string-assembled identifiers; (b) the traversal is the system grep's — tetel deliberately shells out to it rather than reimplementing a dialect — so platform rules about symlinked directories and the -I binary skip bound what a "repo-wide" search physically visited; (c) rooting says where the search started, not which tree it should have been: whether the censused root is the tree the memo designs against stays with the reader, alongside the existing per-root tree-state report; (d) whether anyone read the census is the insincere-examination ceiling — capture makes the extent honest, not the interpretation; and (e) under-declared targets, by construction. The report mechanism for printing exactly this kind of standing limit already exists as the NON_COVERAGE list.

The feature's implementation surface is small and depends on nothing beyond what this memo's facts describe: one additional recorded entry in look_grep, two serde-defaulted structured fields on the extent entry (following world_root's own compatibility precedent), one new append-only record type whose authoring verb refuses uncensused declarations from one dispatch shared by CLI and MCP, one rendered section beside the existing ledger and Facts tables, and one machine check with its human-owed and non-coverage lines. In particular it requires no TET-27 mechanism — no code-to-graph links, no commit references, no dependency propagation — so shipping it first imposes no design debt on that exploration.

The ticket's trigger as written is undecidable in tetel's own record model, verified against the record types: a claim is only { id, proposition, cited fact ids, withdrawn }, a prose block only { heading, level, text, cited claim ids }, and nothing on either surface types a record as a recommendation or an instruction — prose creation is deliberately ungated because "prose is where the author talks, not where they're audited". So "a memo whose recommendation names a target" denotes no set of records any check can enumerate; any implementation of it would have to read English. The claim verb also supplies the refusal precedent the target verb extends: claim already refuses without --cites and on unknown fact ids, so "a structured record must cite a real record of the right shape" is the house's established authoring-refusal pattern.

This design was built against the tetel repository at commit 67191f58c925fcaaed5f9b2ebe218bb23fcded8e ("tet28: pin the census refusal, and make the parity guard real"), with a clean working tree at the start of authoring; the TET-28 modification-target implementation is present in the tree this design reads, and the memo plus its snapshot are the one addition this workspace makes.

TET-29's trigger must be a declaration, not a detection, by the same argument TET-28 implemented rather than merely designed. "Any design or fix that transplants a mechanism from another site" denotes no enumerable set of records: nothing in the record model types a claim or prose block as a transplant, and deciding from English (or from comparing code across two sites) that a fix "transplants" is a heuristic read — the class scope.rs measured dead for symbol mentions ("naming a symbol the code you read calls is normal; concluding about it is the failure; the two are not distinguishable by string matching") and the class targets.rs's shipped doc comment rules out as a refusal trigger. So a transplant is a record the author declares, the refusal attaches to the declaration, and under-declaration is handled the way TET-28 handles it: an always-rendered section that shows its hole, plus a printed non-coverage line, never a detector.

"Transcribed verbatim" cannot be an honour-system field, and does not need to be: the decidable relation is that a premise's text is refused unless it is a verbatim substring of the cited donor fact's captured output. Both sides of that comparison are Strings the tool controls — a fact's output is produced only by look/run (file bytes read verbatim by look_path, grep match lines, a process's merged stream), no authoring surface lets anyone supply output by hand, and output is immutable after mint — so substring containment is a pure byte-level comparison with no normalisation step owned by the check. Typing is the selection mechanism, not the trust: the author types the premise, but a typed premise the donor never wrote fails containment and is refused at the verb. This is exactly the README's Direction item for supporting-span selection ("refused unless it is a verbatim substring of a cited fact — the author cannot type an extent, and here could not invent support, only select it"), and TET-29 is the first place it becomes load-bearing rather than roadmap.

The non-determinism of this check is measured, not merely theoretical, and the disclosure must be carried in the surface rather than left in documentation. The eval recorded that on identical input at temperature 0 the model's reasoning length swings 516..2000 tokens, and that draws reaching the token cap return `finish_reason=length` with content of length zero — so identical mints can produce different `verify` payloads, including a finding on one run and silence on the next. This is a real departure from `attention` and `overlap`, which are derived per call from workspace state already on disk and therefore repeat exactly. The `verify` object must therefore state its own model and a `deterministic: false` marker in every response, so a reader cannot infer parity with the two findings sitting beside it.

The degradation contract is format-level and total: every terminal state of the provider call maps to exactly one `verify.status` value, and no state maps to `ok` with an empty `findings` array unless the model returned a well-formed answer containing no finding. Disabled by config gives `off`; no key in the environment gives `unauthorized`; a transport failure or non-2xx gives `unavailable`; expiry of `verify.timeout_ms` gives `timeout`. An empty or truncated response body is `unavailable` and never `ok`, because the eval measured exactly that state — a draw reaching the token ceiling returns a zero-length body — and because the same eval's harness recorded scoring an error as an answer as one of the two defects that inflated its own results. In every non-`ok` state the mint has already committed, so the contract can never fail a mint or change an exit code.

The strictness objections to byte-level containment dissolve on the actual capture path, and every weaker relation reopens the invention channel. A donor comment wrapped across lines with interior prefix noise (`//`, `*`, indentation) IS a contiguous byte substring of a look_path capture, because look_path stores the file's bytes verbatim — the cost is only that the selected premise carries its comment syntax into the rendered section, which the "never paraphrase" constraint endorses rather than tolerates. Stripping that noise would require knowing each language's comment syntax, which is precisely the hard-coded per-language coupling scope.rs's "language-agnostic by construction" doctrine excludes. Two capture modes genuinely fight containment — grep-derived match outputs interleave "lineno:" prefixes between lines, and whole-search/no-match records carry empty output — so the design's guidance is that a donor fact is minted from `look` of the donor file; that is guidance about which observation to select from, not a new rule, since the relation is indifferent to which kind produced the bytes. Weaker relations fail: per-line containment lets an author stitch non-adjacent lines into a sentence the donor never wrote, and whitespace- or case-normalised matching means the memo shows text the capture does not contain — both are paraphrase with extra steps.

Containment against a fact's whole output has one genuine unsoundness, and it is fixable by the same schema move TET-28 already made. Fact.output is built at mint by joining the buffer entries' non-empty outputs with "\n", and the per-entry boundaries are not stored — so "substring of fact.output" can be satisfied by text straddling the seam between two observations: bytes that were never contiguous in anything the author actually saw, e.g. the tail of one file's capture concatenated with the head of another's. The fix is a serde-defaulted per-entry field on ExtentEntry recording the entry's output byte length, mirroring exactly how kind and pattern were added for TET-28: boundaries become reconstructible from lengths (skipping zero-length entries, matching the mint-time filter), the premise relation is then "verbatim substring of a single observation's output", and a donor fact minted before the field existed is ineligible with the same remedy TET-28 gives legacy facts — re-look and re-mint. Absent means not recorded, never guessed.

The transplant record's shape follows from precedents already shipped, one field at a time. A transplant is an append-only record declared by a new verb (one dispatch shared by CLI and MCP, one new Kind variant and counter): (a) the donor is a citation of exactly ONE fact — the same single-citation rationale targets.rs states ("a target resting on 'one of these several facts' would leave which one undecided"), and a fact citation rather than a typed path because the donor site is then the fact's captured extent, which no author can type; (b) premise rows are verbatim selections from that donor fact's output (per C3-C5), immutable once selected — a selection of immutable bytes has nothing to revise honestly — and withdrawable with --why, mirroring target's withdraw-not-revise discipline; (c) a premise is discharged by citing a claim, in a separate later act, and because `tetel claim` refuses without --cites and on unknown fact ids, a discharge claim rests on at least one real fact by construction — the ticket's "must that claim itself rest on a fact?" is answered yes with zero new machinery; (d) a discharge can be superseded by a later discharge citing a different claim, append-only, so a refuted-and-replaced claim does not strand its premise.

The transplant's destination should be a citation of a live modification target (T#), not a typed path and not an independent record — the two features compose. A transplant installs the donor's mechanism at a site the design necessarily tells the implementer to modify, so under TET-28's own rule that site should already be a declared target; making the transplant verb refuse a destination that is not a live target turns one declaration into a forcing function for the other, and narrows TET-28's admitted under-declaration blind spot for exactly the fix-shape that produced the motivating defect. The composition costs nothing at the edge cases: a green-field destination (new code, new symbol) is still censusable, because censuses() deliberately accepts a NoMatch search — "a symbol with no occurrences is censused by the grep that established it has none" — so declaring a target for a symbol that does not exist yet works today; and the destination-holds claims get a named, censused destination instead of a prose phrase. What the tool cannot verify — that the cited target really is where the mechanism lands — is content, and stays printed as non-coverage rather than guessed at.

An undischarged premise must be a legal workspace state, so the ticket's refusal cannot all move to the verb the way TET-28's did. The instrument works by transcribe-first: the author selects the donor's premises before knowing whether each holds at the destination — the confrontation the section exists to force. Refusing a premise row that cites no claim at declaration time would demand the destination-holds claim exist before the premise can be recorded, inverting that order (answer first, transcribe after) and pushing an author who cannot yet discharge a premise toward not declaring it at all — the same "refusing would make the honest case unwritable to catch the dishonest one" failure scope.rs's discriminator names. TET-28 never faced this because a census either exists or does not; a premise inventory is built across time. So the workspace invariant enforced at the verb is only "every premise is a genuine quotation of the cited donor's capture" (plus: donor fact exists and carries span boundaries, destination target exists and is live, a discharge cites an existing live claim); "every premise is discharged" is not a workspace invariant at all — it is a property of the finished document.

The refusals land on three surfaces, each the earliest that can decide its own question. (1) At the verb: quotation invariants — donor fact exists and is span-eligible, premise text is a verbatim substring of a single observation's output, destination is a live target, a discharge names an existing live claim. These are per-record and decidable at creation, exactly like target's census refusal. (2) At `render --out`: completeness — a live transplant with an undischarged premise (none cited, or its discharge claim withdrawn) refuses the write. This is deliberately later than the verb (the intermediate state is legal while authoring) and deliberately earlier than check (the ticket's placement): --out is the act that writes the reviewable artifact and its snapshot under the pinned policy that a rendered memo is never hand-edited, so a memo with a declared-but-unexamined premise should fail to come into existence rather than exist and fail; the remedy is singular — discharge the premise, or withdraw it or its transplant with --why. A preview render (no --out) still assembles, marking undischarged rows loudly, so mid-work visibility is preserved; this render/--out asymmetry is new, and it is the design's most debatable departure. (3) At check: re-verification of everything above against the shipped snapshot — both directions, since tampering can go either way (a transplant row the snapshot lacks; a snapshot premise whose text is not contained in its donor fact's output; a premise whose discharge claim is withdrawn or missing) — as a machine failure in the same partition as uncensused targets, with rows in a snapshotless document reported human-owed as unverifiable, the standing choice for snapshot-dependent findings. Containment is re-checked byte-for-byte from facts.jsonl, which already ships full outputs; check runs nothing and fetches nothing to do it.

The containment relation was tested against the motivating case itself, at the source, and it passes — with one correction to the ticket's framing. The missed premise ("its parent is remote-known or was walked earlier in this same session", remote_utils.rs:4576 in lonic-forklift at HEAD) is contiguous bytes in a raw capture of the donor file, both as a single clause within one line and as the full seven-line `//` comment with its prefixes, so the verbatim-substring refusal admits it without any comment-syntax knowledge. But the premise does NOT live in the donor function's `///` doc block — collect_changed_closure's doc block never states the insert-before-check discipline or its ordering premise; both live only in the body comment below the signature. So the ticket's phrase "the donor's comment-stated premises" must not be operationalised as "the donor's doc block": the relation has to range over whatever bytes the author captured of the donor site, and a premise stated at a call site or in a body comment is selectable exactly when the author's donor fact folded an observation that covers it — the relation thereby pressures the author to capture the donor widely enough, and a known-but-uncaptured premise demands another look, not a typed row. Separately, today's repaired destination twin states the once-missed condition as one gradeable sentence ("Sound only parents-first — a child that marked a parent-explained hash would otherwise short-circuit the explaining parent's own audit"), which is concrete evidence that the discharge obligation this design demands — one claim per premise, stating that it holds at the destination — fits in a single claim proposition for the hardest observed case.

The rendered section follows compose.rs's shipped conventions with one deliberate difference. A "## Transplants" section renders beside the modification-target section: per live transplant, the donor fact id with its extent labels (labels, never absolute keys — the committed-document rule), the destination target id and symbol, and one entry per live premise carrying the selected text verbatim in a fenced block with the discharging claim id beside it; withdrawn transplants and premises are dropped, and once any claim exists the section renders even when empty ("none declared"), because the hole is the finding — the same visibility answer to under-declaration the target section shipped. The deliberate difference: compose.rs refuses to inline captured output into the document because output is unbounded, but a premise is an author-bounded selection, not a whole capture, so inlining it verbatim is both safe and the entire point — the reader must see the donor's clause on the page, spelled the way the donor's file spells it, or the section is a list of opaque pointers. Fenced blocks rather than table cells because a premise legitimately spans lines and markdown table cells cannot carry multi-line verbatim text without escaping, which would violate byte-fidelity.

What the mechanism cannot catch is boundable and belongs in check's printed NON_COVERAGE list, which exists for exactly this ("a refusal that fired is easily read as coverage it never claimed"). Six entries: (a) a transplant the author never declared — no refusal can reach it; the empty section is its only trace; (b) premises the donor never wrote down — the relation selects from captured text, so a premise that lives in the donor's structure rather than its comments has nothing to select; (c) premises outside the captured extent — a donor fact that folded too narrow a look cannot yield a premise from the lines it never captured; (d) shallow selection — the tool verifies that selected bytes are the donor's, never that they are all the load-bearing ones; selecting one convenient clause and stopping is invisible to any format-level check, because deciding what counts as a premise is design judgment (the ticket says so) and deciding a selection is too small is a truth-check, the insincere-examination ceiling this project registered as permanently out of reach; (e) whether the discharge claim actually addresses its premise, and whether the cited target really is the mechanism's destination — both content; the claim is graded by a grounding pass as written, and the linkage is graded by nobody; (f) a donor comment that is itself wrong — verbatim quotation establishes provenance, never truth. None of these is reachable by a format-level refusal, so printing them is the honest disposition, not a fallback.

The mechanism's value is precisely that it moves one property across check's oldest declared blind spot, and grounding then does the rest. Per the ticket's account of the FORK-94 trail — recorded here as the ticket's report, not re-established — the defective remedy was graded supports twice, correctly, because the violated property was asserted by no claim at all; that situation is exactly the first entry in check's standing non-coverage list, "dependents that never declared themselves", and a grounder that grades propositions as written has nothing to grade where there is no proposition. Every piece of this design funnels toward converting that absent proposition into a present one: the premise row forces the donor's condition onto the page as captured bytes, and the discharge obligation forces a claim that the condition holds at the destination — a claim like any other, resting on facts by construction, entering the evidence ledger, graded by the next grounding pass, revisable and then out-of-proof until regraded. The tool never judges whether the claim is true; it refuses only the shape in which the question goes unasked. And the hardest observed case shows the converted claim fits in one sentence: today's repaired destination states the once-missed condition in a single doc-comment sentence, first-hand evidence that the discharge obligation is one gradeable proposition, not an essay.

The implementation surface is small and every piece extends a mechanism already in the tree: one serde-defaulted per-entry output-length field on ExtentEntry (the same compatibility precedent that added kind and pattern, with the same absent-means-ineligible reading); one new record kind with its counter and id prefix; one transplants.jsonl appended by one CLI/MCP-shared dispatch, shipped by adding one line to snapshot.rs's deliberately-enumerated SNAPSHOT_FILES (whose targets.jsonl entry already documents why a record log must ship: without it the refusal "would hold only inside the workspace that authored the memo"); one rendered section beside render_targets; one completeness refusal in the render --out path; one check re-verifying from files the snapshot already carries (transplant machine findings beside uncensused_targets, unverifiable rows human-owed without a snapshot); and the new NON_COVERAGE lines. Nothing parses any programming language, nothing is re-run at check time, and no aggregate, score, or document-level verdict is introduced anywhere.
This design was taken against tetel at commit e19a4694bedd1bd2bda91626362f9c2d05f35274; every claim below describes that tree.

The environment-only rule for the API key needs one addition to `config.rs` and gets the rest for free. Free: there is no `verify.api_key` in the KEYS registry, and `set` resolves a key through `key_def` and refuses what is not there, listing `known_keys()` so the author is told what they could have written instead — so a key-shaped SETTING is already unwritable. The addition is at the value level: `verify.model`, being a string key, would accept a credential pasted into it, and the strict-when-set half of the asymmetry is the correct hook for a new `Accepts` rule that refuses a credential-shaped value. That refusal is legitimate under the no-heuristic-refusal doctrine because `set` already refuses on value shape by design, and refusing at write time cannot suppress a mint.

Decision — the version. Every threshold in the per-verb table was fitted to one version's probabilities, and no benchmark file records which version answered — where a file names a Jev model at all, it names the alias `jev-latest`. The code names, beside the table, the version the endpoint returned for `jev-latest` on the day of measurement — `typesafe/jev-1.13.0`, recorded from a spike, not from the runs themselves — reads the resolved `model` from every reply, prints it in every response, and adds `typed_model_unmeasured` when it differs from that constant. That flag fails nothing; it states which numbers no longer describe what ran, in the same posture as `deterministic: false`.

The LLM classify call alone costs $0.0054 a draw of the $0.011 the two calls cost together. prop: The comment above `run()` in src/verify.rs says the ratio between `split`'s two calls "is measured nowhere" and implies that the classify call — which "carries the claim text alone" — is the cheap one. On the `claim` verb it is now measured, and the classify call is about half the cost of a `split` verification: $0.0054 a draw on the draws where it ran alone, against $0.011 for classify and check together.

Latency is the binding constraint and it is larger than a per-record estimate suggests, because the unit that pays it is the tool call and not the record. In the largest memo on disk (tet47) the append-only logs carry 33 + 114 + 130 = 277 lines across facts, claims and prose, and 114 of those claim lines resolve to only 39 distinct claim ids — so roughly two thirds of claim traffic is revision. At the eval's observed per-call latency, verifying every line of that run costs tens of minutes of added wall-clock, while the money stays negligible. The design must therefore (a) commit the mint before the verifier runs, so a slow provider delays only the reply and never the record, (b) bound the wait with `verify.timeout_ms` and report `status: timeout` when it expires, and (c) skip the call entirely when a revision does not change the text being compared, which is where most of the volume is.

The first-proof anchor makes the line unclearable by anything that did not look at the prose, and that is deliberate: a further grounding pass over unchanged wording appends records with later timestamps but cannot move the earliest one, so re-grounding never blesses a listed block. The only two things that clear it are reverting the text, and revising or adding a cited claim and having the new wording graded — which is exactly the remedy the finding calls for, since the defect is prose asserting something no claim carries. The cost, stated rather than hidden: a listing has no cheap discharge, so a flow-only edit made after a memo's claims have settled stays listed until the memo's next claim revision, and a memo shipped with such an edit ships the line. This is a smaller version of a cost this project has already paid badly once — `no scope declared` printed one undischargeable line per claim and buried the findings that were about the document under a constant — but it differs where it matters: this line is about *this* document, never fires on all blocks at once, and names two concrete acts that clear it.

Decision — `verify.typed_model` is unset by default, and becomes the default only after one joint run of gate, Jev classify, check and Jev literals on the `claim` corpus shows supports-only claims flagged under 7 of 62, the design's own line, counted per claim. Until then the typed legs reach only an author who set the key: the unsettled comparison of the two classifiers against that line is not a reason to withhold an opt-in configuration whose correct warnings matched the LLM's at 39% of the cost, and it is a reason not to make it what every mint runs.

prop: A capture-time label change necessarily changes the pin: `mint` hashes each pending entry's label, world_root, world_state and output, and does not hash the key. The same observation of the same file at the same tree state therefore pins differently before and after such a change.

The residue is bullets in the existing flat human-owed list, not a new section, and it is identified by document line as well as by block id. The partition has no sub-headings — it is one list of `  - ` entries, some of which already run to several indented lines, as `mint_windows` and `tree_states` do — so a section would be the only one there and would say by its shape that it outranks the rest. One entry per listed block, plus a single preamble entry carrying what is constant across them: that the ordering rests on two clocks nothing here can prove are the same. Printing that constant once rather than in every bullet follows the precedent this crate set when `no scope declared` was collapsed to one document-level line, on the stated grounds that repeating a constant per row "buried the findings that are about *this* document under a constant". The entry names the block's workspace id and the line in this document where its text begins, because `compose::render` never writes a block's id into the output and an id alone names something a reader holding only the memo cannot find; the offsets come from one new function in `compose`, consumed by `render` so that the block-to-line mapping is described in exactly one place. It also names each cited claim, that claim's first-proof timestamp and the pass that wrote it, and the block's own timestamp — the inputs to the comparison, so a reader can disbelieve the conclusion.

This finding belongs to neither of `report.rs`'s two partitions, and that is the answer rather than an evasion of the question. Both arrays are documented as the canonical category names of the MACHINE-CHECKED and HUMAN-OWED partitions of `check`'s output, built from a single enumerated source precisely so the scope strings and the `check` tool description cannot drift from what `check` does. A finding that is produced at mint time, never runs inside `check`, and never enters the record, memo, snapshot or evidence ledger is not a thing `check` can report; adding it to either array would make both partitions' scope strings assert coverage that `check` does not have. Its correct home is the mint result alone.

prop: The residue rule is: a prose block is listed iff (a) it is not a heading and carries at least one citation, (b) every id it cites resolves to a claim in the memo's ledger, (c) every one of those claims is in proof under the predicate `analyze_ledger` already uses — some evidence record whose `proposition_digest` matches sha256 of the claim's current proposition, with the empty digest grandfathered — and (d) the timestamp of the event that set the block's current text is strictly greater than the maximum, over its cited claims, of that claim's earliest in-proof record timestamp. Clause (d) settles the ticket's two ambiguities together: the per-claim anchor is the earliest record grading the current wording, and the per-block anchor is the latest of those, so a block is listed only once its whole evidence base has settled and its text has moved since. Run against the two shipped memos it lists nothing: tet28's and tet29's post-grounding prose revisions each accompanied a claim revision, so the new wording's first proof postdates the edit, and tet28's six post-grounding revisions that did not are heading blocks. Given a FORK-94-shaped edit — tet29's P11 moved 600 seconds past the last first proof with no claim touched — it lists exactly that block and nothing else, and giving one of its cited claims a later first proof clears it.

The implementation surface is six declared modification targets and nothing else: one new field on `Findings`; one new function `prose_after_proof` computing the list from the snapshot's `prose.jsonl` and `claims.jsonl` plus the evidence records `check_file` has already loaded; one call to it inside `check_file`'s existing `if snapshot_dir.is_dir()` block, beside `notes_outside_extent` and `mint_windows`, which is where every snapshot-dependent finding is already computed; one `block_offsets` function in `compose` consumed by `render`; one print loop and one added clause in the human-owed scope sentence in `report::render`; and new entries in `NON_COVERAGE`. `machine_check_failed` is not touched, which is what makes this human-owed by construction rather than by intention. Nothing new ships in the snapshot — `prose.jsonl` and `claims.jsonl` are already in `SNAPSHOT_FILES` — no schema changes, no command is executed and no file the document names is opened, so `check`'s standing guarantees are unaffected. Without a snapshot the list is simply not computed, silently, exactly as `notes_outside_extent` and `mint_windows` are not, and the existing missing-snapshot bullet already tells the reader why. Four things belong in `NON_COVERAGE`: false prose that ships alongside a claim revision, which the ticket concedes and this design does not fix; a paragraph that cites nothing, which has no edge to compare against; whether the two clocks behind the ordering agree; and whether the prose is wrong at all, which nothing here judges.

prop: The vacuous cases are excluded by the in-proof gate rather than by a special case, and the exclusion is justified by non-overlap: a claim with no records at all is already printed as `ungrounded`, and a claim whose every record grades superseded text is already a machine failure as `out_of_proof`, so a prose block resting on either is already in front of the reader under a line that says something truer about it. Requiring every cited claim to be in proof therefore makes a memo with no evidence ledger, and a memo mid-first-draft, list nothing at all — the residue is empty until a memo has been graded, which is when it starts being able to say anything. Two populations fall outside the rule and are worth naming rather than counting: heading blocks, and paragraphs that cite nothing. A paragraph with no citation is the one place a false assertion can sit with no citation edge to compare against, so its invisibility here is a real gap and belongs in the printed non-coverage list, not in a footnote.

There is no digest-shaped alternative in the sharp sense, and the reason is structural rather than an omission: `out_of_proof` can compare digests because a record carries a digest of the very text it graded, whereas nothing in the record shape names or digests a prose block — not `Subject`, not `Predicate`, not `RecordInput` — and the grounding brief deliberately hands a pass only id, proposition and pin. Giving a record a prose digest would require the grounding pass to read the prose it is supposed to grade blind. A weaker, genuinely clock-free alternative is constructible: have `render --out` append a publication record — per prose block its text digest, per claim its proposition digest and whether anything grades it — so the residue becomes an ordinal comparison between successive publications with no clock anywhere. It is rejected on resolution, not on cost. A publication log samples state only at the renders the author happens to perform, so a prose edit and the grading that preceded it inside one publication interval are indistinguishable, and the FORK-94 shape — grounding pass, then fix-round prose, then one render — falls entirely inside a single interval and would be missed. The timestamp comparison resolves exactly that ordering, which is why it is worth its stated bound.

The repository holds exactly 8 committed rendered memos with snapshots, all under docs/design/, and on the build that identifies itself as `tetel 0.1.0 build ac89d5481e9b` every one of them checks at exit 0 with no `provenance-drift` line. The drift baseline this work must not disturb is therefore 0 of 8.

The residue is about any prose whose text postdates the settling of what it cites, not about revision specifically: the block's timestamp is the one that set its current text, whether that was its `Create` or its last `Revise`, both of which carry a `timestamp` on the prose event. Including creations closes an identical exposure at near-zero cost in listings. It is identical because a paragraph written fresh under already-graded claims rests on them exactly as ungradedly as a rewritten one. It is near-zero cost because a paragraph created in a fix round to carry a new assertion normally cites a new claim, and a new claim is not in proof when the paragraph is written; by the time any pass has put it in proof, that first proof postdates the paragraph, so the block never becomes listable. What creation-counting does catch is the case worth catching: a new paragraph written under nothing but old, already-settled claims.

This is the first check to compare timestamps across processes, and the comparison is sound in unit but not in clock. Both sides are produced by a `now_unix` that is byte-identical in the two places it is defined — `SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).map(|d| d.as_secs()).unwrap_or(0)` at evidence.rs:288 and workspace.rs:257, the only two definitions in the worktree — so they are the same unit and epoch, UTC seconds, with no timezone term. What no record establishes is that the two processes kept the same wall clock; `SystemTime::now()` reads the clock of whoever called it. The bound is therefore exact and must be printed rather than implied: an ordering this line reports can be wrong only if the grounding process's clock differed from the authoring workspace's by more than the interval between the prose edit and the pass that first put the cited claims in proof. That interval is the anchor's own doing — first proof rather than last pass puts a whole grounding round between the two events in the case the residue exists for — but nothing in the data bounds it from below, so no claim is made that it is large.

prop: The contract TET-42 should adopt, per artifact: (1) a rendered memo guarantees that every tool-generated extent label citing a file inside the worktree the observation was taken against is spelled relative to that worktree root, and makes no promise about author-typed text or about `proc:` command lines; (2) an evidence ledger inherits that guarantee for `predicate.extent[]` and explicitly keeps `predicate.world[].root` absolute, because it is the identity of the tree, not a citation into it; (3) a snapshot keeps every `key` absolute and canonical, because `key` is what `ExtentEntry::censuses` compares against `world_root`, and stores the same relativized labels the memo renders. This is deliverable because labels and keys are independent fields, the label is built at capture from a `world_root` already on the pending entry, and the only render sites print stored labels verbatim.

prop: "Pin" names two unrelated things in this codebase, and only one of them is affected: a fact's content fingerprint (src/facts.rs), and the document-level "at pin `<hash>`" commit id an author writes into a memo's evidence ledger and src/ledger.rs/src/parse.rs parse into a row's `pin` field. grep does not implement the ticket's first constraint — "an explicitly named path must still be read; only traversal skips" — and delegating that constraint to grep's flags would silently break it. Measured on BSD grep 2.6.0-FreeBSD: a file named explicitly on the command line is skipped when `--exclude` matches it (no output, exit 1, against output and exit 0 for the identical command without the flag), and a directory named explicitly as the recursion root is skipped when `--exclude-dir` matches it (same contrast). Only one of the three cases behaves the way the constraint describes: `--exclude-dir` does not suppress a file inside an excluded directory when that file is named explicitly and searched non-recursively.

The exclusion disclosure can be made durable with no schema change, by writing it into the whole-search record's `label`. Two existing mechanisms carry it from there: `compose::render_facts` builds the committed memo's "Extent (captured)" column by joining extent entries' `label` fields and renders nothing else from an entry — not the `key`, not the captured output — so a label reaches every reader of the committed document; and `facts::mint` hashes each pending entry's `label` (followed by `world_root`, `world_state` and `output`) into the pin, so two searches whose exclusion sets differ pin differently even when their matched output is byte-identical.

A relativized label is only unambiguous if the reader can tell which tree it is relative to, and a rendered memo does not say: `check` on tet61 emits no row naming the memo's world root, only the standing human-owed header sentence about working-tree states. The root survives in the snapshot's facts.jsonl and, by convention, in the author-typed pin claim — neither of which is a mechanism the tool enforces.

`snapshot::check` compares a memo's committed bytes against a full re-render of its snapshot (`rendered == memo_source`), so any change to render output reddens `[provenance-drift]` on every committed memo at once. A capture-time label change cannot do this: `render_facts` prints each stored label verbatim, so an unchanged snapshot re-renders byte-identically no matter what a newer build would have captured.

`brief::build` today performs no filtering — it maps each `Claim` to a `BriefItem` one-for-one — and its doc comment forbids dropping a claim from the brief on account of what its evidence ledger already holds, so any owed-scheduling surface that removed claims from `build`'s output would contradict an invariant already stated in the code.

Owed rules 1 and 2 can be taken directly from `analyze_ledger`'s existing outputs — rule 1 is membership in `ungrounded_claims` (no evidence record at all for the claim id) and rule 2 is membership in `out_of_proof` (records exist, all with a digest differing from `sha256_hex(claim.proposition)`) — with no new predicate over records needed for either.

At the destination the marker's absence disables a specific use with a cheap remedy, exactly as the donor's fields require: an extent entry with no root-relative marker may not be read as openable against the worktree root, only as spelled by whoever captured it, and the remedy is to look again under the new build — cheap because extent and label are immutable per fact but a new observation of the same file costs one `look`.

`analyze_ledger` already holds two different record sets for one claim — `fresh` (digest exactly equals the current proposition digest) and `grading_current` (digest empty OR equal), the latter grandfathering pre-digest records — so the confirmation floor must name which set it counts; counting `grading_current` would let a record that predates the digest field discharge the floor, which under-schedules, whereas counting `fresh` errs toward scheduling.

In an evidence ledger, machine-local paths sit in exactly two places and only one of them can move: across the 8 committed `<memo>.evidence.jsonl` files, 5621 occurrences are in `predicate.extent[]`, which src/evidence.rs builds as `fact.extent.iter().map(|e| e.label.clone())` and which a capture-time label change therefore fixes; 901 are in `predicate.world[].root`, the worktree identity itself; 16 are in a grader's `predicate.note`. No occurrence is in `predicate.source`, `predicate.pin`, `world[].state`, the subject, or any other field.

prop: The ticket's premise for rule 3 — that a claim's pin can change only through a `claim --revise` that alters `--cites` — is false: a claim's pin is not derived from its cited facts at all, but parsed by `find_stated_pin` from a document-level "at pin `<hash>`" sentence in the prose between the nearest preceding heading and the ledger table, and the one parsed value is assigned to every claim in that table.

Because one parsed pin is assigned to every claim under a ledger table, a pin change is a document-level event: rule 3 either fires for every claim in the table or for none of it, so it is a re-pin detector for the memo rather than a per-claim scheduling condition.

Rule 4's "distinct non-author workspaces" count already exists inside `grounding_provenance` as `by_others` — deduped `pass` values of the claim's witnessed records, minus the authoring workspace read from the snapshot's identity — so the floor needs no new notion of workspace identity; it needs that same count restricted to records whose `proposition_digest` matches the current wording, a restriction `grounding_provenance` does not currently apply.

A whole-search record is the one case where the relative form is degenerate: `search_key` stores world_root's own spelling as the key whenever the search root and the worktree root name the same directory — which is precisely the case `ExtentEntry::censuses` requires — so stripping world_root from that key leaves the empty string. The implementation must choose an explicit spelling for the root itself, and the `no-match`/`search` labels additionally interpolate the search root and an exclusion note that enumerates skipped paths in full.

findings.why: The key uses world_root's spelling only when both canonicalizations succeed and compare equal. If canonicalization fails, the code chooses `resolved` instead, so the asserted “whenever” does not hold.

prop: A directory containing nothing but tetel's output is still not "explicitly named", and the cost of that is concrete rather than theoretical. `docs/design` holds exactly nine entries — three rendered memos, three evidence ledgers, three snapshot directories — and nothing else. A search rooted there for the symbol `census` returns 184 lines and 1,200,881 bytes today; under this rule it returns nothing and exits 1. The alternative, treating a directory as named when everything beneath it happens to be tetel's, is a judgement about a directory's contents rather than a test on a path, and the project rules that out as a refusal trigger. So the exclusion stays a format test on the root itself, and the price is that searching across memos requires naming a memo file or a snapshot directory rather than the folder they sit in.

What a committed artifact already survives, and what it does not, are different things. A memo, its evidence ledger and its snapshot copied alone into a fresh git repository at a different absolute path, with an empty state home and no workspaces, already check at exit 0 with no provenance drift — citation ids resolve off-workspace today. What does not survive is a reader's ability to open what a fact opened. Against a clone of this repository at a different absolute path, stripping the worktree prefix from each memo's distinct in-repo absolute paths resolves 32 of 35, 21 of 23 and 32 of 36 to files that exist there; the absolute forms resolve to nothing. A small non-zero residue does not resolve even relativized, and this design did not diagnose it.

The explicit-path exception must be implemented as a decision about whether to pass exclusion flags at all, and `look_grep`'s existing shape already supplies the discriminator. `look_grep` adds `-r` only when `root_path.is_dir()`, and passes `root` through to grep verbatim as the caller spelled it, never canonicalized. So the rule is: when the root is not a directory the caller has named a single file explicitly, and no exclusion flag is passed — which is required, since `--exclude` otherwise suppresses a file named on the command line. When the root is a directory that is itself tetel content, again no exclusion flag is passed — which is required, since `--exclude-dir` otherwise suppresses a directory named as the recursion root. A root counts as tetel content by three format tests and no others: some component of it ends with the literal `.tetel`, or its filename ends with `.evidence.jsonl`, or a directory named by appending `.tetel` to it exists. Only in the remaining case, a directory root that is not itself tetel content, are the three exclusions passed, and each must be spelled the way grep will construct the matched file's name from that same root string.

The confirmation floor and the designer's "stop after the first round that provokes no revision" rule do not conflict, because no rule in that stopping section makes the emptiness of any list a termination condition — the loop stops on machine-clean plus no refuted or unexplained claim, and the round-count rule keys on revisions provoked — so an owed list that is still non-empty at the stopping round is a schedule the run declines to spend another pass on, not an unmet exit criterion.

When the memo's snapshot is absent or carries no `identity.json` — `AuthoringIdentity::NoSnapshot` or `SnapshotWithoutIdentity`, the two cases in which `grounding_provenance` already says the author/grounder distinction "cannot be determined from here" — the confirmation floor is not computable, so the brief's owed list must in those states hold every claim owed under rule 4 rather than counting passes it cannot attribute; this is a format-level condition (the file is present and parses, or it is not) and not a heuristic.

Rule 5's fixpoint is a traversal of the reverse citation graph seeded with the claims owed by rules 1-4, and it terminates on any input — including a citation cycle — by the same `visited`-set construction check 5 already uses for row→row cascades; but the graph must be built over ledger claims, which check 5's `row_citers` deliberately excludes, so the construction is reused while the index itself is new.

There should be no `--owed` flag: because the full brief is emitted either way, an owed section is purely additive and there is no prior behaviour a flag would preserve, while TET-46's stated objection to a flag — that it "leaves no trace in what the caller named, only in how they configured the call" — applies with more force to a brief, the one artifact independence rests on, since two passes running `brief` on the same memo would otherwise receive different documents; the confirmation floor stays a parameter, and the value in force is printed in the brief so that this piece of configuration does leave a trace in the artifact.

Rule 5's matching rule should be the crate's existing `citation_ids_in` rather than a new `C\d+` scan: the existing matcher is already the definition of a row→row citation edge for the dependency-cascade check, it is id-shape-agnostic (a `C\d+` regex would miss real ids of the `R-ROOT` / `CYC-A` shape the crate's own fixtures use, a genuine false-negative class), and its documented error direction is false positives only — which for scheduling means extra grading, never silent under-grading.

TET-28's census predicate needs no change, and this is what makes the two disclosures divide cleanly. `ExtentEntry::censuses` reads exactly five things — that the kind is `Search` or `NoMatch`, that the pattern byte-equals the symbol, that `world_root` is non-empty and not `NO_GIT`, and that `key == world_root` — and never reads `label` or `output`. A worktree-rooted search therefore still censuses after this change, correctly, because the predicate was always about a search's existence and rooting rather than about what it found. What changes is not the predicate but what a passing census entitles a reader to conclude, and that is carried by text: a standing line in `check` saying the exclusion policy exists, and the search record's own `label` saying which patterns this particular search was given.

The donor's exclusion of ledger claims rests on two properties the owed closure does not share — a ledger claim "cannot be a cascade root (no typed `Status`)" and is not a `Row`, so cannot be a row→row dependent — whereas the owed closure roots at owed-ness under rules 1-4, which is defined for a ledger claim and for nothing else, and its dependents are ledger claims by construction; so the exclusion does not carry across, and the index is built over precisely the population the donor omitted.

On the same replay, a rule with no confirmation floor — one workspace-grading per wording — would have retained none of the seven discoveries while cutting workspace-gradings from 69 to 35; N=2 retains five of seven at 51 gradings (a 26% reduction, slightly less than the ticket's estimated 28%), N=3 retains six at 60, and N=4 retains all seven at 67. The floor is therefore what carries the discovery property, and the saving is bought against it monotonically.

The blast radius is bounded and censused. `PendingEntry` is named in source only by src/pending.rs (definition), src/observe.rs (every construction site) and src/facts.rs (the fold in `mint`); `ExtentEntry` is named only by src/facts.rs, src/scope.rs, src/worldstate.rs, src/targets.rs and src/checks.rs, and by no other file under src/; `render_facts` is defined and used only within src/compose.rs, with a single mention in src/ledger.rs. Every other occurrence of all three across the worktree is committed memo prose or verifier-eval evaluation transcripts, not code.

prop: A change confined to `look_grep` cannot alter how an already-committed memo checks, for two independent reasons. The first is call-graph isolation: two exhaustive greps of the whole `src/` tree show `Command::new` matching in only `observe.rs` (the grep inside `look_grep`, and `run_command`'s child) and `worldstate.rs` (git), and `observe::` matching in only `main.rs` and `mcp.rs`, which build a `LookRequest` and dispatch it, and `facts.rs`, where the sole occurrence is inside a doc comment — so every other file in `src/`, including every file on the check and render paths, neither calls into `observe` by that path nor spawns a process by that constructor. The second is immutability: the `tetel fact` module doc states that a revision rewrites the note only, and that "extent, output and pin are set once at mint time and never appear in a revision event at all, so there is no code path that could change them later either". A fact minted under the old behaviour therefore keeps the extent and pin it was minted with, whatever a later `look` would now do.
